title: Pricing Is a Product Feature, Not a Finance Decision
transcript:
Jordan Vance: Marcus, you've run pricing strategy at three companies going through the move from a single flat plan to usage-based pricing. What's the biggest mistake you see?

Marcus Oyelaran-Whyte: Treating pricing as a one-time project instead of a product surface you iterate on. Teams will spend two quarters designing the perfect tiered structure, ship it, and then not touch it again for two years because the pricing page feels scary to change. Meanwhile your competitors, your costs, and your customer mix have all shifted underneath you.

Jordan Vance: Why does pricing feel scarier to change than, say, a UI redesign?

Marcus Oyelaran-Whyte: Because it touches revenue directly and it touches trust. Existing customers notice price changes immediately in a way they don't notice a button color change. But that fear leads teams to under-invest in the thing that has the highest leverage on revenue of almost anything they could build. A five percent improvement in pricing model fit often beats a five percent improvement in conversion rate, because it compounds across every single customer, not just new ones.

Jordan Vance: Walk me through how you actually approach a pricing overhaul.

Marcus Oyelaran-Whyte: Step one is always understanding your value metric, the thing that scales with the value the customer gets. For a project tool it might be active users. For an infrastructure product it might be requests processed. A lot of companies pick a value metric that's easy to measure instead of the one that's actually correlated with perceived value, and then customers feel like they're being charged for something arbitrary. Step two is segmenting customers by willingness to pay, not by company size alone. I've seen five-person companies with huge budgets and two-hundred-person companies squeezing every dollar. Step three, and this is the one everyone skips, is testing the new structure with a small cohort of new signups before rolling it out to your whole funnel, let alone existing customers.

Jordan Vance: What happens when you skip that testing step?

Marcus Oyelaran-Whyte: You find out your new enterprise tier has no clear reason to exist six months later when your sales team can't explain the jump from the mid tier, or you discover your usage-based model creates a bill-shock moment that spikes churn right after a customer's best month. I've seen a company introduce metered pricing and lose their power users first, which is exactly backwards. Power users are the ones with the least price sensitivity if the value is clear, but they're also the ones who notice a confusing bill the fastest.

Jordan Vance: What's a concrete first step for someone whose pricing hasn't changed in years?

Marcus Oyelaran-Whyte: Talk to ten customers who downgraded or churned in the last quarter and ten who upgraded, and ask them to walk you through the moment they decided to change their plan. Don't ask them what they think of your pricing in the abstract, people are bad at that. Ask about the specific decision moment. You'll usually find a pattern, like a plan limit that doesn't match how customers actually grow, within the first six conversations.
